en: In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Commentary*, it is said: "Women take anger as their power, for they must first become angry when they desire to obtain something.
Kings take arrogance and pride as their power. Arhats take diligence as their power. The Buddhas take great compassion as their power."
Regarding strength:
for a bhikṣu, patience is his strength.
Thus, the *Śāriputra-śīla-sūtra* (Yìjiào jīng) says:
One who is able to practice patience may be called a powerful great person.
As the verse of the Seven Buddhas says:
Patience is the supreme path;
the Buddha has said that non-action is the highest form of renunciation. One who harms others is not called a śramaṇa.
Although patience is threefold:
Now, herein we take up the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Why is this?
Because practice is undertaken based upon the sūtras.
Because of the two types of grasping at the non-existence of persons and phenomena,
there are three parts within the text.
First, the capacity for endurance (*kṣānti*).
Second, there is no suffering;
third, there is joy.
This clarifies the capacity for endurance.
Because the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is that which only the Buddhas have fully realized,
it is called the Tathāgata’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Because it cannot be fully fathomed by others,
it is not called a "pāramitā. What is now referred to as the "patience pāramitā" (kṣānti-pāramitā) is [as follows].
These are the Tathāgata’s pure roots of goodness;
they are not the perfections,
nor are they the roots of goodness of those of the two vehicles.
If this is so, then by practicing in accordance with the sutras,
one gives rise to the supreme patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena;
how could one then be weary of the experience of suffering?
Thus the verse says:
One who is able to endure ascetic practices, Because those practices possess virtue, their merit is immeasurable; Such is the most supreme meaning.
"One who is able to endure ascetic practices" means that one is able to endure the ascetic practices undertaken in reliance upon the sūtras.
This is because these ascetic practices possess virtue.
Because this ascetic practice has pure patience as its essential nature consisting of roots of goodness,
it is said that "there is goodness.
As for the statement that "that merit is immeasurable":
The roots of goodness of that patience cannot be fathomed by any other person.
Such is the supreme meaning;
it can be measured only by the Tathāgata.
Therefore it is said: "The perfection of patience is called the non-perfection of patience.
The Sūtra says:
"For what reason? ... up to: because there is no mark of a life-principle (jīva-lakṣaṇa)."
From this point downward, it clarifies the absence of suffering.
This consists of two parts: first, establishing the absence of suffering; second, proving the absence of suffering.
This is the establishment.
The preceding section clarified that one who possesses such [insight] is able to endure;
this section clarifies that because one possesses endurance, there is no suffering.
Why is this? Because if one perceives a distinction between self and other, [suffering arises].
One then perceives the distinction between the harmer and the harmed.
At that time, I practiced in accordance with the sūtras;
since there was no longer any grasping at two selves, [the distinction vanished].
Thus, one does not perceive King Kali as the agent who harms, nor the body as the object that is harmed.
Since these two entities of harm do not exist, from whom could the sensation of suffering arise? It would have to arise from both.
The Sūtra says:
"There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span;
yet there is no mark, nor is it that there is no mark."
Paramārtha says:
"The absence of marks such as selflessness means the absence of intrinsic nature;
'absence of marks' means the absence of other-nature."
Nor is it that there is no sign; it is not that the signs of compassion and wisdom do not exist.
Wuzhuo says: "One who is able to endure is one who has realized the selflessness of phenomena."
Therefore, as the Tathāgata spoke of the pāramitā of kṣānti in the sūtra, according to this,
it refers to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, it says:
How does one know the characteristic of patience? When others direct ill will or the like toward oneself,
one is without the notion of "self" and does not give rise to thoughts of anger.
Nor does one give rise to the notion of existence regarding the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā),
nor give rise to the notion of non-existence regarding that which is not a perfection.
According to this interpretation, there is a slight difference.
Now, it is clear that regarding the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*),
one does not form the notion of "dharma," and regarding that which is not patience, one does not form the notion of "non-dharma.
Therefore, it is said to be signless (*animitta*) and yet not non-signless.
Although these involve harmful matters,
they are subsumed under the patience of reflecting on the Dharma,
as in the case of King Kali.
This should be explained in detail here.
The Sūtra says:
"For what reason? Because in the past, up until the point where one ought to give rise to anger and resentment"—this is the proof.
Furthermore, one clearly understands the meaning of the absence of suffering.
Even when subjected to the extreme act of having one's limbs and joints severed, one does not give rise to anger or resentment; the power of patience is thus fierce.
Hatred arises from the grasping at a self;
since that grasping does not exist,
from whom could hatred arise?
However, hatred (*dveṣa*) is a great delusion,
whereas resentment (*upanāha*) is a minor fetter.
Since it is a great delusion, one may respond to it with a mind intent on killing.
The minor fetters (*paryavasthāna*) may merely be treated with physical pain and poison;
however, because anger (*krodha*) possesses five characteristics, it is termed "great," whereas resentment (*upanāha*) is termed "minor" because it does not possess them.
As explained according to the mind:
the Sūtra says, "Subhūti further recollects the past... up to the mark of being without a life-principle."
This clarifies that there is pleasure.
Since it was previously clarified that there is patience, there is no suffering;
since this clarifies that there is no suffering, there is pleasure.
How so? By practicing patience, the rishi manifests compassion;
by being free from the notion of self, he clarifies the absence of anger.
Because he is free from anger, there is no suffering.
Because there is compassion, there is happiness.
The verse says:
Free from the marks of self and malice, there is truly no suffering or affliction.

"Suffering and happiness; compassion. Thus, the first half of the verse clarifies that there is neither suffering nor the distinction between self and other, while the second half clarifies that there is happiness and the characteristics of compassion and wisdom.
Through compassion there is joy;
through wisdom there is no suffering.
Because compassion and wisdom are conjoined, it is called "shared."
The Sūtra says:
"Therefore, Subhūti, as for those who have generated the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*...
From this point downward, the second section further prevents such faults.
Now, one who perceives suffering while practicing the path of suffering will have a weary mind that sinks into despondency;
whereas one who practices the path of suffering while forgetting suffering [will not].
Thus, the mind becomes light and ascends;
for the purpose of preventing the practice of falling back or sinking,
he teaches the arousal of the non-abiding mind.
The text contains four sections:
first, showing the mind that abides nowhere;
second, showing the object that abides nowhere.
Third, it demonstrates the obstacle of non-abiding;
fourth, it demonstrates the practice of non-abiding.
This clarifies the mind of non-abiding.
Now, enlightenment has non-abiding as its essence.
If one can give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment while forgetting all signs,
the mind will then dissolve into identity with non-abiding.
Therefore, generating the mind of enlightenment while detached from signs is precisely the essence of non-abiding.
As Wuzhuo said:
In order to demonstrate the remedy for the suffering of saṃsāra, it is said that one should abandon all perceptions and so forth.
"Saṃsāra" refers to the wandering through birth and death. If one practices giving while clinging to signs, [it does not counteract the suffering of saṃsāra].
Thus, within the cycle of conditioned existence (saṃsāra), there is the suffering of weariness.
Now, as an antidote to this, it is said that one should be "free from all signs" (sarvanimittāpagata).
The verse says:
To give rise to the mind of non-abandonment, and through practice and steadfastness,
to constitute the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā)— this is the training of the mind that is able to learn.
Regarding "giving rise to the mind of non-abandonment," there are two [aspects].
First, not abandoning the bodhicitta;
second, not abandoning the signless mind.
Therefore, it is said that one should give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining detached from all signs.
This is the non-abandonment of the mind.
A practitioner is one who practices without dwelling upon forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles.
One who is steadfast is one whose practice is firm when detached from signs.
The treatise explains for what purpose one generates the mind and practices: it is for the sake of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
One cultivates that mind capable of training.
As for the perfection of patience:
The Tathāgata is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
One who is able to train the mind is one whose mind is at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
Now, for the sake of seeking the Tathāgata’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), one resolves to practice;
this is the seeking of the mind capable of training in the first stage (bhūmi).
Furthermore, as for the perfection of patience:
The "mind of the first stage" refers to the mind of the first bhūmi.
The "mind capable of learning" refers to the mind prior to the stages (pūrvabhūmi).
Therefore, prior to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), there is no mind of abiding.
Thus it is said: "One cultivates that mind capable of learning.
Therefore, the treatise states:
Entering the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in the first stage (bhūmi) is called the non-abiding mind.
Regarding this "non-abiding":
It does not abide in either phenomena or non-phenomena. Thus, Asanga says:
"Because one does not abide in either non-dharmas or dharmas within the context of selflessness."
The Sūtra says:
"One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on form... up to: one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
This demonstrates the object of non-dwelling.
Do not dwell on forms when generating the mind;
this causes one to leave behind the obstacle of requiting gratitude.
Do not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when generating the mind.
It causes one to leave behind the obstacle of karmic retribution;
one should give rise to non-abiding.
It causes one to leave behind the obstacle of conceptual doubt.
Paramārtha says:
Within this, one should fully possess the abandonment of the three obstacles:
first, the obstacle of one's own body.
Second, repaying kindness;
third, karmic retribution.
Regarding one's own body: if one becomes attached to one's own body, two views immediately arise.
That is to say, the view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism.
Because of eternalism, one does not seek for the future;
because of annihilationism, one does not perceive the future.
This is also the cultivation of the remedy for faults;
the other two can be understood accordingly.
As the Sūtra says:
"If the mind has a dwelling, it is a non-dwelling" indicates the obstacle of non-abiding.
If the mind has a dwelling and dwells upon the two preceding objects, it is a non-dwelling that does not abide in bodhi.
If one possesses such a mind, it constitutes an obstruction.
Paramārtha says:
"If the mind has a dwelling place, it dwells upon the three attachments."
The three types of grasping are:
first, the view of eternalism;
second, the view of nihilism.

Regarding the view of the existence or non-existence of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*): in order to eliminate the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), one does not allow [the mind] to abide in phenomena (*dharma*);
in order to eliminate the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), one does not allow it to abide in non-phenomena (*adharma*).
In order to eliminate the views of existence and non-existence, one is led to abide in the Middle Way.
The former [verse] refutes the ordinary person’s attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as being existent;
the latter refutes the ordinary person’s attachment to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being non-existent.
The final [point] refutes the attachment of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) to the notion that true reality both exists and does not exist.
If one does not depart from these three attachments, one is not in accord with bodhi; therefore, it is said that one "does not abide."
The Sūtra says:
"Therefore, the Buddha spoke of those who have reached the perfection of giving.
This demonstrates the practice of non-abiding.
Now, those who ascend heights must necessarily begin from below, and those who traverse the deep must necessarily start from the shallow.
Therefore, one who wishes to enter the state of the mind that dwells nowhere should cultivate the practice of non-dwelling.
The stage of the non-abiding mind refers to the first bhūmi and above;
the stage of non-abiding practice refers to the period from the path of cultivation (mārgajñatā) down to the preceding stages.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The six pāramitās of the stage of aspiration and delight,
though they are mundane dharmas, are able to induce supramundane states of mind.
Thus says the *Zhendi* (Paramārtha).
The non-abiding mind is the true mind.
If it is associated with patience, its stage is the third bhūmi;
if it is associated with giving, its stage is the first bhūmi.
If one is conjoined with the precepts, one abides in the second stage.
From the fourth stage upward, one should understand according to their respective meanings the qualities of diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, the power of vows, and gnosis.
Because one does not abandon this true mind,
one leaves behind all marks and arouses the resolve to practice. Generally speaking,
from the first bhūmi upward, these are consolidated into four types of saṃgha, all of whom cultivate the six pāramitās together.
First, the shameless monk, which refers to one who has violated the precepts;
second, the sheep-like mute monk.
This refers to: first, the ordinary person who observes the precepts;
second, the Sangha with a sense of shame, which refers to those of the two vehicles; and third, the Sangha of the ultimate truth.
This refers to true bodhisattvas:
in the first three stages, they cultivate mundane modes of practice;
being the same as ordinary beings in their inability to reach definitive resolution, they are likened to mute sheep.
Next, in the fourth stage, one cultivates supramundane aspects of practice;
being identical to those of the two vehicles, one refrains from further committing evil, which is likened to having a sense of shame.
In the subsequent three stages, one cultivates practices that transcend both the mundane and the supramundane.
Because this bodhisattva does not depart from the path of manifold practices within his own stage, he is called the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha).
This same judgment must be applied to all pure lands that contain ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
If one discusses this according to ultimate reality,
there are no longer ordinary beings or followers of the two vehicles within the Pure Land; thus,
the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) says:
Women and those with impaired faculties do not give rise to the seeds of the two vehicles; yet,
from the perspective of provisional characteristics, they do exist.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies the three grades and nine ranks;
thus, even ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles attain rebirth there. Pappha said:
The pure lands of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha contain ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles,
whereas the pure lands of the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha do not.
Thus says Paramārtha.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles perceive Amitābha Buddha within a defiled land;
the various bodhisattvas perceive Amitābha Buddha within a pure land.
According to these two explanations:
The land of retribution is exclusively pure,
whereas the land of response is both defiled and pure.
As the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.
From this point downward, there are two sections concerning non-abiding and the severing of doubt.
The first concerns the severing of doubt.
Second, regarding the abandonment through one's own practice,
an external interlocutor raises a doubt:
"If there is no abiding, for whose sake does one practice?"
If one were to see sentient beings as being capable [of action], they would be called "sentient beings who dwell in attachment.
Now it is clarified that, from the perspective of the conventional, one may say there is "action," whereas from the perspective of the ultimate truth, there is nothing that is done.
The verse says:
Practice for the sake of sentient beings; thus one should recognize the causes, the sentient beings, and their affairs, as well as detachment.
The first half clarifies the conventional;
the second half clarifies the ultimate.
The text contains two layers.
First, it is in terms of the conventional; second, it is in terms of the ultimate. This refers to the conventional.
"One should practice giving in this way for the benefit of all sentient beings" means:
This is because, according to conventional truth, sentient beings exist and can therefore be described as conditioned;
thus it is said that one should practice giving in this way for the benefit of all sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases exist according to conventional truth,
that which is called "benefit" is analyzed as the three types of giving (*dāna*); that is,
it causes sentient beings to ascend [to liberation] by relinquishing the three kinds of suffering.
One attains three kinds of happiness.
Through the generosity of material requisites,
one causes the abandonment of the suffering of poverty and the attainment of the happiness of great wealth.
By means of the gift of fearlessness,
one causes others to abandon the suffering of fear and attain the happiness of security; by means of the gift of Dharma,
one causes them to abandon the suffering of saṃsāra and attain the happiness of nirvāṇa.
The reason a bodhisattva is able to benefit sentient beings through the three kinds of giving (dāna) is that six are genuine while one is semblance; thus,
they are able to benefit sentient beings.
The six truths refer to benefiting sentient beings through the six perfections. By means of generosity,
one causes them to become vessels of goodness.
By means of ethical discipline, one causes them to observe restraint;
by means of patience, one counteracts malice;
and by means of diligence, one assists them in accordance with what is wholesome.
One causes them to enter the Dharma by transforming them through meditative concentration;
one cuts through their web of doubt with wisdom.

As the verse says: "Causing [them] to become fit vessels, forbidding [evil], enduring evil, assisting in the good, causing entry into the Dharma, and cutting through doubt—these six types of activity bring benefit."
Regarding the seven "semblances":
first, the semblance of a mother;
second, the semblance of a father.
Third, resembling a virtuous friend;
fourth, resembling a companion;
fifth, resembling a robust servant; sixth and seventh, resembling a preceptor (*ācārya*).
There are seven types of pseudo-upādhyāyas.
Each of these seven has five activities;
together, they constitute thirty-five kinds of beneficial service.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-vyākhyāna*,
because a bodhisattva is able to possess the six true [perfections] and seven semblances,
they are able to benefit sentient beings.
It is said that one should practice giving in this manner for the benefit of all sentient beings.
The Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata has taught that all marks, when examined to their ultimate limit, are not sentient beings."
This refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The intent is to clarify that, from the perspective of the ultimate truth, one may say there is no abiding.
Why? Because all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute the substance of sentient beings.
Sentient beings are merely the name "sentient beings.
Their various characteristics are not characteristics;
their essence is empty and lacks substantial reality.
Sentient beings are not truly born; they are called "empty.
Yet, even this provisional designation is empty in its essence.
What, then, could they abide in?
Therefore, the verse says:
The conventional designation and the aggregates— The Tathāgata is free from those characteristics;
In all Buddhas, those two do not exist, Because they perceive the true Dharma.
Examining this, the first two phrases concern true non-abiding,
while the latter two phrases demonstrate the meaning of non-abiding.
"The absence of those two" refers to the absence of both name and substance.
The rest is self-evident.
Asaṅga states: "Because it is not that sentient beings do not exist."
When sentient beings encounter opposition, they become weary;
therefore, [the Buddha] reveals the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.
According to this, it refers precisely to the true non-abiding.
Paramārtha says:
"There are two kinds of provisional names (prajñapti):
first, general names."
This refers to names of the six realms of existence and secondly,
specific names, namely those given by one's parents.
These two names cannot be found apart from the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses;
therefore, "name" is a conventional designation.
Furthermore, apart from name-and-form, the sense organs and consciousnesses also cannot be found.
If one is separated from the four great elements, form (rūpa) is likewise unobtainable.
One cannot thereby establish that this object does not exist;
because the object does not exist, consciousness (vijñāna) does not exist.
Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is absent, both the designation and the substance of sentient beings are entirely non-existent.
The absence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the absence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The absence of consciousness is the absence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Since both are empty,
what is there to be delivered? Therefore,
it is said that when one accords with the truth, there is nothing to be done.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth... up to... one who does not speak otherwise.
The preceding section clarified non-abiding with respect to external transformation.
This refers to the non-abiding as elucidated by oneself.
An objection is raised:
"If the Way is non-abiding, it should not serve as the cause for the fruit."
If one abides in the fruit, how can they also be called "non-abiding"?
Herein it is clarified that although the Path does not abide,
it is nonetheless able to serve as a cause.
This is what those who have realized the truth say regarding that which is "penetrated," while outsiders say it is "that which can be reached.
One should simply rely on my words;
by taking them as a basis for faith, one may practice according to the sacred teachings.
The text has two layers:
first, the exhortation to believe;
second, the prevention of transgressions.
This is an exhortation to faith.
The five phrases are intended to clarify four meanings.
"True speech" refers to the teaching of true wisdom.
He speaks of suchness according to reality;
he speaks of the principle of the Four Truths with truthful speech;
and he records the events of the three periods of time without deceptive speech.
The single statement "not different" definitively establishes that the preceding four [turnings] are irreversible.
Thus, the verse says:
Although the fruit does not abide in the path, the path can nevertheless serve as its cause.
By the true words of all Buddhas, that wisdom is of four kinds;
however, the first two lines clarify that both cause and fruit are without abiding,
for the fruit does not abide within the cause because it is free from signs.
Because they are free from characteristics, they do not abide in the fruit.
Although each does not abide, cause and effect succeed one another; this is abiding within non-abiding.
Question:
Is the dwelling of non-dwelling not itself a dwelling?
Answer: [It is.]
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), there is cause and effect, attainment, and the discussion of abiding and non-abiding;
from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is clarified that there is no cause and effect, no attainment, and no discussion of abiding or non-abiding.
Therefore, Asaṅga said:
From the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there exist cause and effect as well as awakening (bodhi).
The next two lines provide a general indication of five terms.
The verse says:
Real wisdom and the Hīnayāna, the teaching of the Mahāyāna dharma and all predictions of enlightenment— because these are spoken without falsehood,
"real wisdom" refers to true speech.
The Hīnayāna is speech that accords with reality;
the Mahāyāna is speech that accords with suchness;
all those who have received predictions of enlightenment are those whose speech is non-deceptive.
"Speaking without falsehood" means that one's words do not differ from reality.
Wuzhuo says: "Speaking the truth" is for the purpose of manifesting the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Truthful speech" (*satyavādin*) is for the purpose of manifesting the practice of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
because there exist both afflictions and purification.
"As-it-is speech" (*yathārtha-vādin*) is for the purpose of [manifesting] the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Not speaking otherwise constitutes the practice of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
because there exist both afflictions (*kleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).
According to the preceding two statements, it is clearly taught that the conventional is real.
The latter two phrases clarify that the teaching is true and not false.
Paramārtha states:
"True speech" refers to the Tathāgata’s own solemn vow.
There are two aspects to this self-vow.
First, it clarifies that regarding the Wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata,
none among all those in the world— whether Brahmins, celestial Māras, or others— [can turn it back].
No one is able to overturn what I have spoken.
Second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata establishes the ten titles;
[none among] all the world’s brāhmaṇas, celestial Māras, and so forth [can do so].
No one can destroy this name;
because it speaks of reality, it is called "True Speech.
As for "Real Speech," in terms of the Hīnayāna, it refers to the Four Noble Truths and the three gates of liberation.
All phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature;
being empty, they are signless;
being signless, they are wishless.
This is explained solely in terms of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Although there are three names, they collectively constitute a single essence;
because this explains reality, it is called "true speech" (*satya-vacana*).
Regarding the "speaker as it is," this refers to the Mahāyāna explanation of the three natures and the three non-natures,
which is the true suchness (tathatā) of the emptiness of phenomena;
that is to say, the three gates of liberation.
Because these three gates are able to eliminate the three obstacles,
the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"Knowing the nature of conceptual differentiation (parikalpita-svabhāva) leads to the realization of the gate of liberation that is emptiness."
It can eliminate the afflictions of the flesh;
by knowing the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), one penetrates the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha) and can eliminate the afflictions of the skin.
Knowing the nature of reality, one penetrates the gate of liberation that is signless;
this can eliminate the afflictions of the mind—
the first being the obstacle to liberation, followed by the obstacle to meditative concentration.
Subsequently, there is the obstruction to omniscience (*sarvajñāvaraṇa*). Upon awakening from these three obstructions, one realizes suchness (*tathatā*);
because one speaks in accordance with suchness, one is called "one whose speech is such" (*tathāgata*).
One who does not speak deceptively records the events of the three periods of time without any error or delusion;
this differs from other people, who may be either attached or detached.
These four types of speech all derive their names from their respective objects.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
This is to prevent error.
Having already raised these words to encourage faith, there may be those who,
out of fear, cling to the literal words and thereby lose the Way;
it is to prevent this that [the following is said].
Now, this is countered:
this "Dharma" refers specifically to the teachings of the Tathāgata.
This Dharma is that which is universally accessible through the discernment of the Buddha's teachings.
This is what has been spoken through the eloquence of the Buddha;
because it accords with the Buddha,
it is the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata.
Now, the Way dwells in wordlessness;
to cling to words is to lose the Way.
Therefore, this Dharma has no reality.
However, it is said that while words can indicate the path, one does not see the path apart from words.
Therefore, this Dharma contains no empty talk,
for it is able to indicate the path.
The analogy of the finger pointing at the moon is employed because the Way is beyond words;
the metaphor of abandoning the boat is likewise composed for this reason.
The verse says:
In accordance with that true knowledge, it is taught as being neither unreal nor real;
like taking realization from hearing the sound, it is taught as the antidote to such [views].
The first half establishes the thesis;
the second half explains its meaning,
by means of the Tathāgata’s discourse.
It is not false because it accords with ultimate wisdom;
it is not real because the realization of principle is beyond words.
It serves as the antidote to taking what is heard as literal sound and grasping it as realization.
To speak thus means that at the time of listening to the Dharma,
one is free from the two types of grasping.
In order to refute the attachment that claims "this is the path" or "this is not the path," it is said that the teaching of the antidote is thus proclaimed.
Therefore, Asaṅga says:
"In the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening and in its exposition, there is neither reality nor falsehood.
It is not real because its nature is not existent as expressed in words."
Consider that the essence of verbal expression is void and its intrinsic nature is empty.
That which is non-delusory does not exist with an intrinsic nature as verbal expression suggests.
Thus, although verbal expression is empty, [it functions].
The principle revealed [by this] exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Paramārtha states that there are three meanings to the phrase "neither real nor unreal."
First, the realized and the unrealized;
second, the reached and the unreached;
third, the manifestation of actual reality.
The initial intention is this:
to grasp the principle by relying on a text whose meaning is fully understood is not false;
however, to grasp the principle by relying on a text whose meaning is not fully understood is not real.
As for the subsequent meaning:
if one seeks through words and is able to reach the Way, then it is not false;
yet because the locus of the Way transcends words, it is not real.
Regarding the latter intention,
as for the statement "it is not real," it is indeed non-real.
Regarding the statement "it is not false":
it is indeed not false.
Since both the false and the real are established as real, this then manifests true speech.
However, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata contains both the definitive and the provisional.
This is as explained in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on the Explanation) regarding the four intentions and the four reliances.
First is the intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*).
As it is said regarding the former Buddha Vipaśyin, and so forth—
such statements are made by taking as a basis the equality of cause and effect within the Dharmakāya.
Second, the meaning of the specific sense:
as it is said that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, and so forth;
according to the preceding [context], this was taught for the sake of the two vehicles as the selflessness of persons.
Now, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, I teach the dharma of selflessness (*anātman*).
However, my previous teaching on the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) was intended in a distinct sense: the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Third, the intention regarding another time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*).
For example, it is said:
"If anyone aspires to see Amitābha Buddha, they shall all attain rebirth [in his land]."
This is because they will attain birth at another time;
such are the four distinct intentions.
That person possesses such roots of goodness.
Whether the Tathāgata praises or [reproaches], it is because those [actions] are slight [in nature]; therefore, such cases as these are so designated.
Now, as for the meaning of these four "intentions" (*abhiprāya*):
whether a matter is real or false, they are alike designated as "intention" because they are directed toward a specific purpose; hence the name "intention."
Establishing [the two] marks is for the purpose of destroying the eight obstacles.
The intention of equality is for the purpose of destroying the obstacle of disparaging the Buddha. Some say:
Because of this, you give rise to such notions of arising and ceasing; thinking that since arising is immediately followed by cessation,
the Buddha is the same as yourself, you consequently develop a sense of contempt.
To shatter this [view of] the equality of the self, [it is said]:
"The past Buddha Vipaśyin was none other than my own body;
how could he be subject to the same arising and ceasing as you?"
The purpose of establishing this distinct meaning is to refute the obstacle of disparaging the Dharma. Someone says:
Even infants are able to see forms and hear sounds;
what difficulty is there in understanding the meaning of human speech, principles, and dharmas?
It is for the sake of destroying this obstacle.
The teaching on the three natures is realized upon entering the stage of the Dharma;
this establishes the intention of "another time" to break the obstacle of indolence.
Some, upon hearing that one must practice for a long duration before being born in the Pure Land,
immediately give rise to indolence;
it is to destroy this obstacle that [the following is taught].
The statement "□□□ gives rise to non-retrogression" establishes a distinct intentional meaning to refute the latter five obstacles.
First, it breaks the obstacle of having few desires.
Since [the practitioner] has already failed to maintain the precepts,
one must disparage giving and praise the precepts.
Second, it destroys the obstacle of greedy conduct;
that is, it refers to praising the Pure Land while being attached to the objects of greed.
Third, it destroys the obstacle of arrogant conduct.
This refers to clinging to one's own land as being the "knee" [of the Buddha-field];
thus, one must purify the wondrous Pure Land.
Fourth, it destroys the obstacle of regretful conduct.
This refers to the case where [Devadatta] pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha; because he did not perceive the foul odor [of his own karma], he gave rise to affliction.
Therefore, it must be said that even by performing acts of non-benefit toward the Buddha, one can still be reborn in the good realms.
The text [proceeds to] clarify the deeds of the Buddha.
This should be explained in detail here.
Fifth, it is for the purpose of destroying the obstacle of indeterminate nature.
There are those who hold that the followers of the two vehicles are not destined to become Buddhas.
To destroy these obstacles,
it is necessary to explain the prophecy of enlightenment and the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Among these five [points],...
Because they all first praise and later disparage,
this refers to the intention of "desire.
Regarding the four reliances:
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Ornamentation) is titled in four sections.
The first is the section for causing [entrance],
which teaches the śrāvakas to enter into the meaning of the Dharma so that they do not fear the existence of form and other [aggregates].
According to this, one should realize that persons have no self.
This is the section on the two characteristics:
within the three natures—such as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—there is no essence and no arising; their intrinsic nature is pure.
Because it explains all phenomena (*dharma*),
it causes the bodhisattva to realize that phenomena are selfless (*anātman*).
This is the third section on remedies.
Based on the severance of all faults through the counteractive remedies for obstacles,
this applies generally to the aforementioned two types of persons.
For the sake of those of the Lesser Vehicle, it is taught that by means of the gates of liberation, they shall be led to leave behind the four categories.
For the sake of the Mahāyāna, the *tathatā* (suchness) is taught so that one may be freed from the eight categories and the four secret nodes;
for it is by relying on profound speech and indirect expression that the true meaning is attained.

This treatise is for the purpose of refuting the heterodox schools... [omitted] ...not firm, but firm and stable, well-established in the midst of inversion... [omitted] ...as for "not firm," it refers fundamentally to the afflictions.
Now, regarding the phrase "to perceive within the non-solid that which is solid": this means that one does not emerge from [the cycle of existence], which is what is called "understanding."

"Perverted" refers to [the views of] permanence, bliss, [self, and purity]. If one were to [correctly] understand these, one would immediately become a noble one (*ārya*). This is because the name "well-abiding" is common [to both];

if one adheres to the [perverted] examples, one is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), but if one understands the [correct] examples, one becomes a noble one. As for those "afflicted by afflictions," the term "affliction" designates both persons and phenomena; because they are afflicted by afflictions, they do not transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The Bodhisattva, for the sake of [the various marks], takes them as the name for "enjoyment," because he enjoys the dharma-bliss.
Therefore, Paramārtha said: "[They are] truly existent; [those who do not understand this] fail to reach it."
Because this is truly without basis for clinging to the false,
[the mind] gives rise to views;
because the mind dwells in attachment, it cannot attain the state of being neither pervasive nor non-pervasive.
It is simply because [ignorance] is extinguished, just as great darkness is dispelled by light;
for the delusions of the mind are like great darkness,
which can only be eliminated when a Bodhisattva ascends to the stages (*bhūmi*).
If a bodhisattva’s mind dwells [upon anything],
they will fall into the ten perceptions and be unable to realize the seventeen emptinesses, becoming like one who is blind and in darkness.
The ten perceptions and the seventeen emptinesses are as explained in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, in future ages, down to those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it.

From the beginning of the first chapter, the general purport has primarily elucidated the Sūtra; from this point until the subsequent inquiry into its meaning, the intent is to manifest the practice of cultivation.
There are two aspects to the practice:
first, the actual cultivation;
second, the exhortation to cultivate meritorious deeds.
There are four sections:
first, teaching the cause;
second, demonstrating the fruit.
Third, the inferior is censured;
fourth, the superior is revealed.
This is the cause of the teaching.
This refers to the place for practicing this sutra;
it concerns the matters of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and practicing.
There are two kinds of practice.
There are two meanings for each phrase.
Regarding the phrases, there are three kinds: first, receiving; second, upholding; and third, reading and reciting.
The meanings likewise consist of three.
First, hearing from others;
second, internal reflection;
third, practicing according to the teaching.
By virtue of this meaning, two further qualities are established:
first, that of the teacher, who is able to benefit others;
and second, that of the practitioner, who is able to benefit themselves.
The Dharma is manifested through the benefit of oneself and others.
There are two types of persons and three types of dharmas;
the latter two manifest the signifier (*vācaka*).
This refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
which are the words themselves;
second, it reveals that which is expressed by those words.
This refers to the path and its fruit;
that is, the meaning of practice.
Regarding the three types of persons:
First, the ability to uphold;
second, the ability to explain;
third, the ability to practice.
The practitioner benefits themselves by maturing their own roots of virtue;
the teacher benefits others by maturing the roots of virtue in others;
and the upholder benefits both self and others.
Because one recites them for oneself and explains them to others,
there are ten types of correct practice when both text and meaning are considered together.
The first is writing.
Second, making offerings;
third, transmission and circulation;
fourth, the truths.
Fifth, reading for oneself;
sixth, memorizing and retaining;
seventh, reciting for oneself.
8. Extensive exposition;
9. contemplation;
10. [omitted].
